questions.prompt: What scorecard correction does Chapter 4 make first?
choices: The cleanest-looking plan is always the best one
Simple optics can still miss the real economics
Debt automatically makes a business smarter

explanation.gentle: Thorndike says a neat story can still be weaker if it ignores how value is really created.
explanation.direct: The chapter starts by challenging the idea that simplicity is automatically superior.
explanation.competitive: Clean is not the same as economically strong.

questions.prompt: Why is TCI's setting structurally difficult in this chapter?
choices: Because the company sits in a fast-moving, debt-heavy cable environment
Because the business has no financing choices at all
Because the chapter stops caring about operations

explanation.gentle: The industry is moving fast, debt matters, and structure affects value.
explanation.direct: TCI's setting forces the reader to consider leverage and design as part of the economics.
explanation.competitive: The business moves too fast for lazy scorecards.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter treat leverage?
choices: As a moral vice that should always be rejected
As a disciplined tool that can sharpen or damage results depending on the economics
As a status symbol for sophisticated managers

explanation.gentle: Debt can help or hurt. The chapter only respects it when strong economics govern it.
explanation.direct: Leverage is useful here as a governed instrument, not as a badge.
explanation.competitive: Debt magnifies truth before it magnifies style.

questions.prompt: Riley has one financing plan that looks cleaner and another that preserves more value. What fits Chapter 4 best?
choices: Choose the cleaner plan because it is easier to defend
Choose the structure with stronger economics if the logic stays clear and auditable
Reject both plans because any complexity is suspicious

explanation.gentle: The chapter says better economics can justify a harder-looking structure.
explanation.direct: Choice B matches Malone's logic: the real test is retained value, not tidy optics.
explanation.competitive: Take the ugly winner only if it survives the audit.

questions.prompt: Which belief does Chapter 4 challenge most directly?
choices: Every complicated plan must be smarter than a simple one
A simple-looking plan is always the strongest discipline
After-tax outcomes are irrelevant

explanation.gentle: Thorndike pushes against the idea that easy-to-explain always means better.
explanation.direct: The chapter attacks simplicity worship, not caution itself.
explanation.competitive: Respectable neatness can still be lazy analysis.

questions.prompt: Ethan's debate team resists a more layered prep system even though it improves results. What is the chapter's best diagnosis?
choices: The team is correctly avoiding all complexity
The team is mistaking clean optics for stronger economics
The team should add more layers until nobody understands the system

explanation.gentle: The team prefers the cleaner story even though the new structure works better.
explanation.direct: This is Chapter 4's problem in miniature: neatness is outranking outcome.
explanation.competitive: They are choosing the prettier tool over the sharper one.

questions.prompt: Why does tax-aware structure matter in this chapter?
choices: Because owners only keep pre-tax value
Because after-tax outcomes are part of the real scorecard
Because tax talk automatically proves sophistication

explanation.gentle: The structure matters if it changes what value owners actually keep.
explanation.direct: Thorndike treats after-tax outcomes as real outcomes, not decorative details.
explanation.competitive: Ignoring taxes is just ignoring a leak.

questions.prompt: What is the anti-camouflage rule in Chapter 4?
choices: Complexity deserves trust only when it clarifies value instead of hiding it
Every layered structure should be hidden from criticism
The hardest plan to explain is usually the smartest

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps one plain test: does the design make the economics clearer or murkier?
explanation.direct: Complexity only counts when it still answers a visible value scorecard.
explanation.competitive: If scrutiny makes the case fuzzier, the sophistication is fake.

questions.prompt: What makes Malone's complexity defensible rather than performative?
choices: It is complicated enough that outsiders cannot question it
It improves the economics while remaining answerable to a plain value standard
It uses more debt than simpler rivals

explanation.gentle: The chapter only respects the complexity if it creates stronger value and still stays understandable.
explanation.direct: Malone matters when difficult tools remain auditable under the scorecard.
explanation.competitive: The structure has to get stronger the harder you look at it.

questions.prompt: If Chapter 4 is about honest complexity under a clear scorecard, what is the strongest bridge into Katharine Graham's next chapter?
choices: How can disciplined judgment survive in a human succession story where authority is inherited rather than engineered?
How can every future case avoid structure completely?
How can managers hide all difficult choices inside finance language?

explanation.gentle: The next natural question is how outsider discipline works when the challenge is inheritance and confidence, not structural finance.
explanation.direct: This is the right bridge because the next case turns from design complexity to judgment under succession pressure.
explanation.competitive: Malone proves intelligence can survive the mess. Graham will have to prove it can survive inheritance.
